World.title: ‘Total war’: The human face of the assault on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia is intensifying its war with a new generation of deadly drones, turning everyday life into a daily gamble for Kyiv’s traumatised inhabitants.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are times at night when Svitlana Dvorchina will not leave her apartment when the air-raid alarm goes off. It can be more secure to stay at home, she feels, rather than join the rush to a shelter. And her two young children can be so tired from playing in the afternoon that they sleep through the noise. “They don’t hear it,” she says. “Even when we have these massive night attacks on Kyiv, for example, my kids can sleep well. But me, I do not sleep that way. I hear every explosion.” A woman walks near the scene of a Russian air raid on a warehouse on the outskirts of Kyiv. AP Photo/Francisco Seco Dvorchina, 36, has moved all their beds to a corner of the room so they are as far as possible from the windows, in case a blast sends glass flying. Like so many in the Ukrainian capital, she thinks about the danger from drone and missile strikes, and she knows she can wake the children and run to a damp basement or a crowded underground metro station. Often, her decision is to stay with Eilisai, 11, and Artem, 6, and let them sleep. She remembers what her husband, Yurii, told her earlier in the war: “Do not run away. Just be home.” She has to do this on her own. Yurii, a professional soldier, died from cancer six months ago. Svitlana Dvorchina with her sons Eilisai, 11, and Artem, 6. Kateryna Bludova We are talking at a care hub where parents can give their children an escape from the war. Eilisai and Artem are in a library down the corridor with a crowd of other kids listening to stories. Dvorchina speaks with an incredible calm about the choices she has to make as winter approaches, even though the options are fraught: she cannot afford the rent with Yurii gone, and she is not sure if the heating will work.



“It’s hard to explain what this is, but it’s definitely not life. It’s surviving.” Olena Klochik Every decision is a gamble when Russia is intensifying its drone and missile strikes. In Kyiv, people talk about “total war” from Russian attacks on civilian targets like petrol stations, passenger trains, buses and homes. Ukrainians continue their lives despite the air raid alerts, trying to make the most of every peaceful moment, but the pressure is exhausting after more than four years of war. Kyivites pause to observe Ukraine’s daily national minute’s silence in memory of those killed in the war. AP Photo/Francisco Seco Olena Klochik weeps when she describes life under Russian attack. “It’s a fear. It’s not a life. It’s surviving,” she says. “What we do is we try to catch a moment of life between air alarms.” Her tears fall as she talks. Her younger brother, Maxim, a soldier, died in eastern Ukraine one week ago. He left a trench in the fighting around Pokrovsk to rescue a wounded comrade, only to be killed by a landmine. Their mother has been asked to supply a DNA sample so he can be formally identified. A woman rides an e-bike as firefighters work to extinguish a burning pharmaceutical warehouse attacked by Russia. AP Photo/Francisco Seco



Klochik, 37, is angry and distraught as she speaks about the cruelty of the war. Her three children, Kyrylo, 14, Sofiia, 10, and Petro, 9, are in the library with the others while we talk. Here at the care hub, operated by Caritas Ukraine and supported by donations from Australia, there is at least a respite from hardship. “Our children have to study in the shelters,” says Klochik, speaking through a translator. “They always have to be somewhere hiding. Here, at Caritas, I come for my children to distract them from the war. And here we are all together, and we do something to help our children. “It’s hard to explain what this is, but it’s definitely not life. It’s surviving.” Olena Klochik says Ukraine desperately needs foreign support to end the war. Kateryna Bludova There is exhaustion in her voice, although her words do not sound like despair. She says Ukraine cannot rely on US President Donald Trump and should get more help from Europe to stop the Russian attacks. “We are invincible,” she says. “But to finish this war, we need support from other countries.” The total war on civilians is not new to anyone who remembers the casual killing of Ukrainians in the towns around Kyiv after Russian soldiers embarked on the full-scale invasion in February 2022. But the war is very different after the arms race of the past four years. Now, civilians are targeted from the air on a dangerous new scale. A woman looks out from a wrecked apartment in a residential building. AP Photo/Francisco Seco



Iryna Peliukhnia, the co-ordinator of the Caritas care hub, is lucky to be alive. She hid in a cellar with her husband and two children when Russian soldiers occupied her village near Kyiv during the assault on the capital in February 2022. They had little food for two weeks, as the temperature fell below zero. Now she worries about what the cold will do to families in Kyiv in the months ahead. “The families who come to Caritas are now frightened of what they will face this winter,” she says. Iryna Peliukhnia co-ordinates the Caritas care hub for families and children in Kyiv. Kateryna Bludova Ukraine is more exposed to ballistic missiles because it lacks enough of the Patriot interceptors that can protect its cities. It is more exposed to faster drones because it cannot match the speed of the new Russian weapons fitted with turbojet engines from China. Months may pass before Ukraine can deploy more powerful drone interceptors. This means energy systems are vulnerable just as the cold sets in. Ukrainian air defence officers estimate the Russians launched 2800 jet-powered drones at targets in August, almost twice the number seen in the previous month. The Ukraine Conflict Monitor, an independent service run by Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, estimates there were 4700 drone strikes of all types on Ukraine in August. The new weapons, capable of flying at 600km/h, are becoming a bigger part of the Russian arsenal. At this rate, Russia could devastate civilian targets with jet-powered drones in the months ahead.



The threat ahead Winter could bring a humanitarian disaster. Many residents have been without heating in their apartments after gas and electricity outages over the years. Some talk of temperatures falling to minus 10 degrees inside their homes, let alone out on the street. Families often go to government centres, known as Points of Invincibility, to get hot water, charge their mobiles, connect to the internet or collect basic first-aid kits. Euheniia Kravtsova with her children Alina, 5, and Oleksii, 7. Kateryna Bludova This is where Euheniia Kravtsova, 26, takes her two children on most days. “We spend a lot of time there,” she says. “Sometimes there is heating at home, sometimes not. It’s unreliable. After school, we go to the Point of Invincibility. We have a meal there, then we go home to spend the night.” Leaving Kyiv is an option for some families, but rents are high in the safer cities to the west, and work is not easy to find in the quiet villages away from the conflict. For Kravtsova, who works as a cleaner, moving west is out of the question because it would mean being even further from her husband, Denys, who is stationed with the armed forces in the east. Their daughter, Alina, 5, cries during some of the attacks. Their son, Oleksii, 7, wants to serve like his father. Blackened buildings stand testament to Russia’s four-year onslaught on the Ukrainian capital. AP Photo/Dan Bashakov Kravtsova explains all this with a soft smile. “It’s not as difficult as it could be,” she says. She is from Dobropillya, an eastern city under constant Russian fire, and she fled to the capital with the children two years ago. In Kyiv, at least, they are more secure.

World.title: Forget the romance. Rugby Australia and NZ Rugby are locked in a marriage of necessity
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionRugby Australia Forget the romance. Rugby Australia and NZ Rugby are locked in a marriage of necessity Paul Cully September 19, 2026 — 9:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The romantic view of the recent rapprochement between Rugby Australia and New Zealand Rugby is that it reinforced old fraternal bonds that cannot be broken – a sign of the enduring respect and affection between the parties. The cynical view is that their shared challenges have brought them back together: their huge financial issues and the presence of the NRL, a cashed-up and aggressive rival. New Zealand and Australia have worked together to get the Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test off the ground. Getty Images A confidential NZ Rugby document I obtained earlier this week painted the governing body’s issues in stark terms. A forecast loss of $NZ27 million ($21.75 million) this year. A structural deficit of $NZ20 million a year, with no end in sight without change.



A projected loss of $NZ66 million in 2027-2031, despite a British and Irish Lions tour windfall in 2029. Also, the document reveals: “The NRL now draws 28 million NZ viewing hours against Super Rugby’s 19 million and NPC’s [National Provincial Championship] 14 million.” The Warriors are going from strength to strength in New Zealand. Getty Images That last line means rugby competitions in New Zealand are still more watched than the NRL despite Warriors-mania (and the viewing figures exclude All Blacks Tests), but you get the point: rugby league is a big thing across the ditch. These figures would be all too familiar to Australian rugby fans, and gallows humourists might conclude that Australia was always 10 years ahead of New Zealand.



What this all means for Australia is unclear. Powerbrokers from across the New Zealand rugby system will descend on Wellington next week to discuss their options, but identifying the issue is the easy part – finding agreement on a solution is far harder. However, there is a half-glass-full world in which the urgency of the Kiwis’ problems works in Australia’s favour. Rugby Australia CEO Phil Waugh with NZ Rugby counterpart Steve Lancaster at the Super Rugby Pacific launch earlier this year. Getty Images Certainly, there doesn’t seem to be any appetite from NZ Rugby to bin Super Rugby Pacific and return to a domestic competition, the NPC, as their elite competition model. The NZ Rugby document states that the preferred men’s elite competition “retains Trans-Tasman, with design able to expand”.



So, for example, if you are a private investor keen to put money into the NSW Waratahs, there is certainty that the Tahs will have a competition to play in. And, for example, if you are the Queensland Rugby Union and contemplating a split between the professional game and the community game with a view to investing into the Reds in a private Super Rugby model, that possibility still exists. But above and beyond the specifics, the common challenges facing Australia and New Zealand should promote a collegial attitude to addressing them. There is evidence that is already happening, with the Reds and Blues set to face each other on the Anzac Day weekend in Brisbane. A Bledisloe Cup Test will serve as the main event on April 25. The Herald has spoken to Reds chief executive David Hanham and his Blues counterpart Karl Budge in recent weeks, and both are on the same page about the opportunity that fixture presents, rather than looking at the Wallabies and All Blacks who won’t be available.



“I think we’ve got to reverse how we view these occasions,” Budge said. “I look at someone like young Cohen Norrie [Auckland and Blues five eighth/fullback]. In almost any other sport, he’d be considered a first-round draft pick. “When those first-round draft picks get a chance to finally debut for a club, it’s a sellout occasion in other sports. Super Rugby Pacific is forecast to lose about $NZ11 million in the 2025-2026 financial year. Getty Images “I’d rather reverse that conversation and go, ‘Isn’t it amazing that we’re going to finally get a chance to see Cohen Norrie rather than see Beauden Barrett’.” The other Super Rugby clubs will share similar attitudes regarding the preceding weekend, when they will also be missing their Test players.



The Wallabies and All Blacks will, of course, remain the primary teams for RA and NZR, the only outfits that actually make a bit of money. Related Article Australian rugby Waratahs’ firebrand could become a Springbok-style asset, says coach But both unions need to find a way to make a professional rugby competition below Test level at least sustainable from a commercial perspective. At present, it clearly is not. The NZ Rugby document revealed that Super Rugby Pacific is forecast to lose about $NZ11 million in the 2025-2026 financial year, while their Super Rugby Aupiki competition for women’s rugby will lose an eye-watering $NZ8.5 million.



NZ Rugby’s reduced broadcast deal with Sky is partly to blame, despite the robust viewing figures Super Rugby Pacific still attracts. Getting that competition right will be no mean feat, but RA and NZ Rugby are both now in the same position: they have to, or else. World.title: Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House Michael Koziol Updated September 19, 2026 — 6:38am ,first published 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump said he was banning cable news channel CNN and two other prominent US media outlets from the White House because of what he referred to as their “constant ‘reporting’ fake news”. The US president made the declaration on his social media platform Truth Social on Friday afternoon (Saturday morning AEST). He said MS-NOW, formerly known as MSNBC, was also banned, along with politics-focused news outlet Politico – which has just launched an Australian division. US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Friday afternoon. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote. He said the ban would be effective immediately. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”



The announcement is an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s long-standing animosity towards the media and outlets that report factual stories he does not like. It was not immediately clear exactly what Trump’s directive meant, as there are various levels of access that reporters have to the White House and the president. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in the White House press briefing room on the night a shooter targeted the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. AP Journalists are issued passes for the White House grounds, but that does not guarantee access to the “pool” - a smaller, rotating group of reporters that are allowed inside the Oval Office. CNN’s Kristen Holmes was still present and reporting from the White House on Friday afternoon.



Asked for clarification at a news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said: “I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. The ban would go as far as you can.” Trump suggested there was no particular trigger for his decision to ban the three outlets now. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said. “They purposefully write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.” Donald Trump takes questions from reporters in the Oval Office on Friday after announcing a ban on CNN, Politico and MS-NOW. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The president went on to cite his election victory and wins in all seven swing states, and suggested the banned outlets did not extend him enough praise. “I won [in] a landslide and I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart, I get it a little bit from Fox [News]. What I do ask is just a semblance of truth … everything’s been a victory. It has all been a victory.”



At one point, Trump was confused when a reporter attempted to ask him about the ban. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” he said. He later acknowledged: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” In his first term, Trump attempted to ban a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, by revoking his White House pass. CNN succeeded in having it restored via a legal challenge. CNN’s Kristen Holmes at the White House in April. She was still reporting from the White House grounds on Friday afternoon after the “ban”. Getty Images But in Trump’s second term, the White House has taken more control of the daily press pool, giving space to smaller, “new media” outlets that are typically conservative or even far-right. The White House Correspondents’ Association has traditionally managed the pool. WHCA president Jacqui Heinrich, who is from Fox News, said the group stood in defence of its colleagues at CNN, MS-NOW and Politico, who were being “singled out for doing their jobs”.



“The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” Heinrich said. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organisation’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask. “This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.” The White House press pool in the Oval Office on Friday. Bloomberg Founded in 1980, CNN provides close coverage of US politics, with several prominent reporters ordinarily based at the White House. Owned by Warner Bros Discovery, it is set to be sold to David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance as part of a $US110 billion ($154b) merger, though Paramount recently said selling the channel was an option to resolve market concentration issues in the deal. Trump has frequently targeted CNN for its coverage of his war against Iran and other matters. He has directed many attacks at high-profile anchor Kaitlan Collins, whom he called “very dumb and unhappy” last week. He regularly accuses her of failing to smile sufficiently.



Politico’s inclusion on the banned list was surprising given it is not a regular Trump target. In his Truth Social post, he dredged up an old complaint about the outlet receiving $US8 million from the Biden administration, suggesting it was “corruption”. In fact, the money was for subscriptions to Politico’s premium products. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer CNN said it stood behind its White House team and its fair and accurate reporting. “We have right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” the network said. “Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right.” There is currently no White House press secretary after Karoline Leavitt departed the role last month. She has not been replaced. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: How this team of experts guides 80-metre turbine blades down our roads with just millimetres to spare
World.content:
It is just after midnight on a winter morning when we gather at the Port of Newcastle.

In the background coal ships slink by, in the foreground an almost inconceivably vast wind turbine blade lies along the spine of a truck bed like some sort of alien life form strapped to a gurney in a sci-fi film.

It’s so big that it’s hard to fit it all into the frame of your eye from any reasonable perspective. At its tip it tapers to the length of schoolkid’s ruler. Towards that tapered end it has a jagged edge like a cartoon dragon’s teeth, a shape designed to reduce noise as it slices through the air. Peering up at its midsection, you could be looking at a warship’s prow from the ocean’s surface.

A team of transport specialists are making last-minute preparations to move this beast through the sleeping streets of suburban Newcastle and the coal villages of the Hunter Valley, along the Golden Highway to a hillside outside Wellington on the NSW Central Slopes, where it is to be raised upon a tower as part of a Squadron Energy wind farm that will soon be generating enough electricity for about 220,000 homes.

It seems absurd that this thing can be moved at all, let alone along busy roads, but the man in charge of this circus, Steve Spiller, seems impossibly calm. Jovial, even.

The police and pilots gather before the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Form and function

Wind turbine blades, explains engineer Dr Rosemary Barnes, are the largest single-component objects that humans regularly either build or seek to move. Artefacts of the modern world tend to shrink as technology advances, but wind turbines, shaped by both economic and physical forces, keep growing.

Longer turbine blades scoop up more wind and generate more electricity with each rotation, says Barnes, who has spent a career designing, building and repairing turbines and blades around the world and now runs a renewable energy consultancy. A dozen huge turbines need fewer gearboxes, less cable and wiring, less maintenance, less concrete and steel to generate as much electricity as dozens of small ones.

As the turbines grow in length, so do the forces exerted upon them. In extreme conditions, a large blade might bend 10 to 15 metres from a straight line. Imagine, says Barnes, a diving board wilting under the weight of a herd of elephants.

“They have to survive that transfer of force hundreds of millions of times over a life of about 30 years. Every time the blade is in the three o’clock position, gravity is bending it one way, and then when it goes into the nine o’clock position, it’s bending the exact opposite way, and it keeps repeating like that as it spins. It’s just like if you bend a paperclip back and forth repeatedly, you know that small load is not going to break it, but you do it enough times, and you get fatigue loading, it is going to break.”

All this means that not only must a blade be handmade from tough, light composite materials, they are stronger when they are crafted in a single piece, rather than disassembled for transport, which brings us back to Spiller and his crew in Newcastle.

The monster they are about to move is 82 metres long and weighs just over 20 tonnes.

The port

The crew is doing last-minute checks on vehicles and equipment. Craig Carpenter is inspecting the Kenworth truck and the purpose-built trailer he is about to drive. The trailer has a long spine that can be extended to suit its load, and six sets of axles at the rear.

The steerer, Freddie Scheepers, checks the truck prior to the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Tonight Carpenter’s load from front grille to blade tip will be 92 metres long. Carpenter picked up the nickname Blade Runner One for his smooth driving while moving blades in Western Australia last year, but just as crucial is Freddie Scheepers, who is “steerer” and will pursue Carpenter in a van close behind the truck.

Scheepers must not only keep his own vehicle on the road, but when necessary will use a remote control to steer the rear axles of the trailer. He keeps in constant contact with Carpenter so at any given moment the two know exactly where the blade tip is in relation to the road and the rest of the rig.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond. They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.” Steve Spiller, project manager

When the front of the rig moves upwards and is forcing the tip towards the ground, Scheepers will also be able to raise and lower the blade itself, the last metres of which rest in a hydraulic jack that sits over the axle sets.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond,” says Spiller, watching Carpenter and Scheepers make final preparations. “They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.”

Mayfield Macca’s

The convoy pulls out at about 1am. There are two police cars, as required by law when moving a load of this size in NSW. There are four pilot vehicles which help manage traffic around the truck and trailer. Scheepers’ steering van hunts along behind the blade like a sheepdog, and we follow in a four-wheel drive with Spiller, the project manager.

The turbine blade starts its journey from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Also in tow is a Transport NSW vehicle with a couple of observers, there to see if anything can be learnt or improved for future runs. After this, there are still another 195 blades to go, let alone the turbine hubs, tower sections and generators.

“When you pull back the curtain, this is what building a wind farm looks like – thousands of individual movements, decisions and people are needed to get every component to site,” Squadron Energy’s chief executive Rob Wheals later observes.

Steve Spiller, Ares Group project manager, accompanies the turbine blade on its journey from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

“At 80 metres long and shaped like a banana, each blade is one of the most challenging pieces of infrastructure to ever move.”

From Spiller’s radio we can hear occasional chatter from the pilot vehicles, but he leaves the “Bladerunners” to their own quiet comms channel so they can concentrate. Before we’ve even left the port precinct the blade tip sweeps out over a cyclone fence, clearing it by what seems like centimetres.

Spiller doesn’t flinch. Every move is rehearsed, every distance measured.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side on its journey from the Port of Newcastle to the wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

At a McDonald’s on a roundabout on Industrial Drive in the neighbouring suburb of Mayfield, the cop cars and pilot vehicles splay out to halt traffic coming from three directions, and Scheepers climbs out of his van to flick a switch on the rig to remote control. He adjusts the height of the suspension, and then he steers the rear of the rig around the turn.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side at the intersection of Industrial Drive and Maitland Road, Mayfield. Photo: Janie Barrett

Speed picks up, at least until the caravan reaches the Hunter Expressway. To make it onto that section, the pilots block traffic on the expressway in both directions while the Bladerunners navigate the rig 80 metres down an off-ramp into what would otherwise be oncoming traffic, then drive a kilometre down the wrong side of the road before crossing back. Spiller seems pleased by how smoothly this dance of traffic and truck is performed.

The remote used for steering the rear of the truck that carried the enormous turbine blade. Photo: Janie Barrett

As we head northwest towards the Golden Highway, Spiller relaxes enough to tell his story. He became an expert in moving big stuff almost by accident. At 19, he took a job with a logistics firm and began moving shipping containers. Half a decade later he was moving wind turbine parts, and the work took him around the world with the global giant GE. He has moved bits and pieces of wind farms by sea and land and even air, at one point chartering the world’s biggest aircraft, an Antonov, to move a wind turbine hub and six generators from Leipzig to Adelaide.

In Germany, near the Polish border, he recalls coaxing blades through tiny villages on a truck that could raise them to near vertical from the base to navigate tight spaces.

Freddie Scheepers changes the steering of the rear of the truck from manual to automatic via an external switch on the truck. Photo: Janie Barrett

In Australia, it’s easier because we have so much space. “I moved 300 blades through Toowoomba without complaint,” he boasts. Today he works for the Ares Group, which was contracted by GE, who built the blade at a factory in China, to shepherd it safely off the ship in Newcastle and on to the Squadron Energy site outside Wellington.

Despite the late hour you can tell the convoy is having an impact along the way. In one hamlet we pass within metres of the old coal miners’ cottages. A man in a dressing gown watches on in the pre-dawn from his veranda. His expression is impossible to read in the revolving lights.

Craig Carpenter, the truck driver who drove the turbine blade from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

From the sections of widened road you can see along the way the years of preparation that went into this operation. EnergyCo, the NSW government authority responsible for delivering the state’s five renewable energy zones, has spent $130 million preparing this route.



Inland

There are rules about moving oversized loads in the dark on the Golden Highway, so the convoy pulls over before dawn. A quiet pall descends across the still convoy, except for cheerful noises from Carpenter’s cabin. He hums and sings to himself and taps out a rhythm before drifting into silence.

In bright early light, against the country homes in Denman, the enormity of the blade begins to become clearer. It is longer than whole blocks of the little town. Along the Golden Highway, the convoy at times creeps up to something approaching normal traffic speed, and time passes quickly until we reach the site of the wind farm, headquartered on a sheep and cattle operation on rolling green hills east of Wellington.

As the truck prepares to tackle the narrow dirt roads built for the project we are taken into a sprawling site office for a safety induction. Whiteboards on the walls show the progress in the construction of each of the 69 turbines that will soon be operational here. There are posters boosting the “core values” of Squadron Energy, which is owned by Tattarang, the investment company that is in turn owned by Andrew Forrest and Nicola Forrest. The values include “Humility” and “Frugality”.

It is midafternoon on a hilltop I had last seen two years earlier when Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Forrest attended a sod-turning ceremony. Bladerunner One finally steps out of his cabin and offers up a great two-armed stretch to the sky. By now Spiller has left the site on his way back to his head office in Melbourne. Workers on-site scramble over the blade, breaking it free of its harnesses and lowering it into a cradle by a half-built tower. By the time it is operational it will stand 148 metres from base to blade tip.

There’s no getting around the impact the project is having on a beautiful landscape. Construction pads are scraped into the ground by each tower and the new roads hum with the sort of traffic flow you’d expect in a prosperous town.

The turbine blade arrives ar the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Later I ask farmer John Holland, owner of Uungula, for which the wind farm is named, what he makes of it all. He speaks with a careful, precise manner, aware of the controversy that wind projects attract. Squadron, he says, will clean up after the construction is complete, leaving him with new roads, giving even better access to the property’s ridge lines.

He says he has no fear about the impact of the turbines on his stock. Visiting other wind farms, he has seen sheep “camping” under the towers for shade. He reckons the turbines look majestic, but admits that when he saw renders of what they would look like spread across the land he loves he found it “a little confronting.”

He thinks renewable energy is a part of the solution for Australia’s growing energy demand, but not the only one. Like many farmers, he opposes grid-scale solar plants taking up agricultural land. But he has practical considerations too. The rent Squadron will pay for each turbine will let the family retire a fair chunk of debt, though he won’t say how much. Nor will he say how many turbines his farm will host. “That’s a bit like asking how much money I’ve got in the bank. It’s a bit rude.”

But he is happy to say the income has helped settle the questions of succession that can cause such grief to farming families, and to update equipment and improve fences and dams.

“It’s the confidence to be able to run the property the way it should be run.”

I ask him what Uungula means.

“It’s an Aboriginal word,” he says. “It means wind in the hills.”

Workers unload the turbine blade after its long journey. Photo: Janie Barrett

World.title: Trump, Denmark strike deal to expand US military presence in Greenland
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations Trump, Denmark strike deal to expand US military presence in Greenland Michael Koziol September 19, 2026 — 10:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Denmark, the United States and Greenland are expected to sign an agreement that will allow the US to increase its military presence in the Danish territory and ban adversaries such as Russia and China from building bases or making sensitive investments there. The agreement was simultaneously announced by all three parties and will be signed at the United Nations next week when world leaders converge on New York for the UN General Assembly’s high-level meetings. Greenlanders protest in front of the US consulate in the capital, Nuuk, in January. Getty Images It is a significant win for US President Donald Trump, who made Arctic security a key plank of his foreign policy agenda, but frightened European allies with his demands for the US to purchase Greenland or perhaps take the Danish territory by force. Based on details provided by a US State Department official, the deal stops well short of giving the US control over Greenland, but expands American access and puts explicit, permanent restrictions on the presence of NATO adversaries.



It guaranteed the US the “complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent”, the State Department official said, including permanent access, basing and overflight rights. Related Article Mining Trump has big hopes for Greenland – Australia just gave him a reality check “This agreement ensures the necessary US military presence in Greenland permanently, allowing the US military to increase the number of bases in Greenland as required.” Under the deal, a non-NATO country would not be allowed to build a military base or maintain a troop presence in Greenland, and only the US and its allies could make sensitive investments in Greenland. The US had raised concerns about Chinese investments in the territory, although experts have said these claims are inflated, with most of China’s purported projects there failing or never materialising.





Trump, meanwhile, called it a “dream come true” and said the US would immediately begin developing a large military presence in an appropriate part of the territory. “For over 100 years, [US] Presidents have known the strategic importance of Greenland, but NONE of them were able to do anything about it,” Trump said on social media. “I am proud to be the President that permanently and conclusively addressed this very important situation.” Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen (left) and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen in 2025. AP Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who played a key role in the negotiations, called it a “huge win” for the US and the American people. “Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defence area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” he said.



“This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: World rowing hoses down premier’s ‘signed, sealed and delivered’ Rocky claim
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRoad to Brisbane 2032 World rowing hoses down premier’s ‘signed, sealed and delivered’ Rocky claim Catherine Strohfeldt September 19, 2026 — 9:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just days after the state government trumpeted an apparent victory over its Rockhampton Olympic rowing course, the sport’s international bodies have dampened down the premature party. On Friday evening, a joint statement from World Rowing, alongside Paddle Worldwide, Rowing Australia, and Paddle Australia said the state’s as-yet-unreleased independent report on the Fitzroy River course was not the final step of a full international sign-off. “As part of the next phase of venue planning, which includes the project validation report process led by the Games Independent Infrastructure Coordination Authority (GIICA), several additional elements are requested to be confirmed,” World Rowing said in a statement. Fitzroy River has to be assessed on several “technical details” before state and global rowing bodies accept it as an Olympic rowing venue. Sylvia Liber These “technical details” included confirmation that athletes would have access to services and facilities, the rowing bodies said.



“We look forward to continuing to work closely with all stakeholders on requests and updates ahead of 2032,” the statement read. On Thursday, when the state announced the findings from the independent report – carried out by WaterProof Marine Consultancy – Premier David Crisafulli said both World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide had endorsed the course. The premier said it passed its assessment “with flying colours”, and that the state’s hand-picked venue was “signed, sealed and delivered”. However, under pressure to release the full report, the government withheld it on Friday, drawing ire from Queensland’s rowing community.



QRowunion chairman Gary Merritt said Thursday’s announcement echoed premature assurances by Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie that the Rockhampton course was suitable while the state watched it flood. Related Article Road to Brisbane 2032 Secrecy over Olympic rowing course fuels south-east rower backlash “I’m sure there is a lot more to what’s going on. This government pulled the same stunt back in March and announced it was all signed, sealed and delivered,” Merritt said. “They’ve done the same again now.” On Thursday, Bleijie said the Fitzroy River course had to clear a few checks and balances, including the ongoing GIICA project validation report.





Concerns about the central Queensland course included its distance from the Olympic host city, as well as available facilities for athletes. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Total war’: The human face of the assault on Ukraine
World.content:
Russia is intensifying its war with a new generation of deadly drones, turning everyday life into a daily gamble for Kyiv’s traumatised inhabitants.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are times at night when Svitlana Dvorchina will not leave her apartment when the air-raid alarm goes off. It can be more secure to stay at home, she feels, rather than join the rush to a shelter. And her two young children can be so tired from playing in the afternoon that they sleep through the noise. “They don’t hear it,” she says. “Even when we have these massive night attacks on Kyiv, for example, my kids can sleep well. But me, I do not sleep that way. I hear every explosion.” A woman walks near the scene of a Russian air raid on a warehouse on the outskirts of Kyiv. AP Photo/Francisco Seco Dvorchina, 36, has moved all their beds to a corner of the room so they are as far as possible from the windows, in case a blast sends glass flying. Like so many in the Ukrainian capital, she thinks about the danger from drone and missile strikes, and she knows she can wake the children and run to a damp basement or a crowded underground metro station. Often, her decision is to stay with Eilisai, 11, and Artem, 6, and let them sleep. She remembers what her husband, Yurii, told her earlier in the war: “Do not run away. Just be home.” She has to do this on her own. Yurii, a professional soldier, died from cancer six months ago. Svitlana Dvorchina with her sons Eilisai, 11, and Artem, 6. Kateryna Bludova We are talking at a care hub where parents can give their children an escape from the war. Eilisai and Artem are in a library down the corridor with a crowd of other kids listening to stories. Dvorchina speaks with an incredible calm about the choices she has to make as winter approaches, even though the options are fraught: she cannot afford the rent with Yurii gone, and she is not sure if the heating will work.



“It’s hard to explain what this is, but it’s definitely not life. It’s surviving.” Olena Klochik Every decision is a gamble when Russia is intensifying its drone and missile strikes. In Kyiv, people talk about “total war” from Russian attacks on civilian targets like petrol stations, passenger trains, buses and homes. Ukrainians continue their lives despite the air raid alerts, trying to make the most of every peaceful moment, but the pressure is exhausting after more than four years of war. Kyivites pause to observe Ukraine’s daily national minute’s silence in memory of those killed in the war. AP Photo/Francisco Seco Olena Klochik weeps when she describes life under Russian attack. “It’s a fear. It’s not a life. It’s surviving,” she says. “What we do is we try to catch a moment of life between air alarms.” Her tears fall as she talks. Her younger brother, Maxim, a soldier, died in eastern Ukraine one week ago. He left a trench in the fighting around Pokrovsk to rescue a wounded comrade, only to be killed by a landmine. Their mother has been asked to supply a DNA sample so he can be formally identified. A woman rides an e-bike as firefighters work to extinguish a burning pharmaceutical warehouse attacked by Russia. AP Photo/Francisco Seco



Klochik, 37, is angry and distraught as she speaks about the cruelty of the war. Her three children, Kyrylo, 14, Sofiia, 10, and Petro, 9, are in the library with the others while we talk. Here at the care hub, operated by Caritas Ukraine and supported by donations from Australia, there is at least a respite from hardship. “Our children have to study in the shelters,” says Klochik, speaking through a translator. “They always have to be somewhere hiding. Here, at Caritas, I come for my children to distract them from the war. And here we are all together, and we do something to help our children. “It’s hard to explain what this is, but it’s definitely not life. It’s surviving.” Olena Klochik says Ukraine desperately needs foreign support to end the war. Kateryna Bludova There is exhaustion in her voice, although her words do not sound like despair. She says Ukraine cannot rely on US President Donald Trump and should get more help from Europe to stop the Russian attacks. “We are invincible,” she says. “But to finish this war, we need support from other countries.” The total war on civilians is not new to anyone who remembers the casual killing of Ukrainians in the towns around Kyiv after Russian soldiers embarked on the full-scale invasion in February 2022. But the war is very different after the arms race of the past four years. Now, civilians are targeted from the air on a dangerous new scale. A woman looks out from a wrecked apartment in a residential building. AP Photo/Francisco Seco



Iryna Peliukhnia, the co-ordinator of the Caritas care hub, is lucky to be alive. She hid in a cellar with her husband and two children when Russian soldiers occupied her village near Kyiv during the assault on the capital in February 2022. They had little food for two weeks, as the temperature fell below zero. Now she worries about what the cold will do to families in Kyiv in the months ahead. “The families who come to Caritas are now frightened of what they will face this winter,” she says. Iryna Peliukhnia co-ordinates the Caritas care hub for families and children in Kyiv. Kateryna Bludova Ukraine is more exposed to ballistic missiles because it lacks enough of the Patriot interceptors that can protect its cities. It is more exposed to faster drones because it cannot match the speed of the new Russian weapons fitted with turbojet engines from China. Months may pass before Ukraine can deploy more powerful drone interceptors. This means energy systems are vulnerable just as the cold sets in. Ukrainian air defence officers estimate the Russians launched 2800 jet-powered drones at targets in August, almost twice the number seen in the previous month. The Ukraine Conflict Monitor, an independent service run by Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, estimates there were 4700 drone strikes of all types on Ukraine in August. The new weapons, capable of flying at 600km/h, are becoming a bigger part of the Russian arsenal. At this rate, Russia could devastate civilian targets with jet-powered drones in the months ahead.



The threat ahead Winter could bring a humanitarian disaster. Many residents have been without heating in their apartments after gas and electricity outages over the years. Some talk of temperatures falling to minus 10 degrees inside their homes, let alone out on the street. Families often go to government centres, known as Points of Invincibility, to get hot water, charge their mobiles, connect to the internet or collect basic first-aid kits. Euheniia Kravtsova with her children Alina, 5, and Oleksii, 7. Kateryna Bludova This is where Euheniia Kravtsova, 26, takes her two children on most days. “We spend a lot of time there,” she says. “Sometimes there is heating at home, sometimes not. It’s unreliable. After school, we go to the Point of Invincibility. We have a meal there, then we go home to spend the night.” Leaving Kyiv is an option for some families, but rents are high in the safer cities to the west, and work is not easy to find in the quiet villages away from the conflict. For Kravtsova, who works as a cleaner, moving west is out of the question because it would mean being even further from her husband, Denys, who is stationed with the armed forces in the east. Their daughter, Alina, 5, cries during some of the attacks. Their son, Oleksii, 7, wants to serve like his father. Blackened buildings stand testament to Russia’s four-year onslaught on the Ukrainian capital. AP Photo/Dan Bashakov Kravtsova explains all this with a soft smile. “It’s not as difficult as it could be,” she says. She is from Dobropillya, an eastern city under constant Russian fire, and she fled to the capital with the children two years ago. In Kyiv, at least, they are more secure.

World.title: Forget the romance. Rugby Australia and NZ Rugby are locked in a marriage of necessity
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionRugby Australia Forget the romance. Rugby Australia and NZ Rugby are locked in a marriage of necessity Paul Cully September 19, 2026 — 9:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The romantic view of the recent rapprochement between Rugby Australia and New Zealand Rugby is that it reinforced old fraternal bonds that cannot be broken – a sign of the enduring respect and affection between the parties. The cynical view is that their shared challenges have brought them back together: their huge financial issues and the presence of the NRL, a cashed-up and aggressive rival. New Zealand and Australia have worked together to get the Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test off the ground. Getty Images A confidential NZ Rugby document I obtained earlier this week painted the governing body’s issues in stark terms. A forecast loss of $NZ27 million ($21.75 million) this year. A structural deficit of $NZ20 million a year, with no end in sight without change.



A projected loss of $NZ66 million in 2027-2031, despite a British and Irish Lions tour windfall in 2029. Also, the document reveals: “The NRL now draws 28 million NZ viewing hours against Super Rugby’s 19 million and NPC’s [National Provincial Championship] 14 million.” The Warriors are going from strength to strength in New Zealand. Getty Images That last line means rugby competitions in New Zealand are still more watched than the NRL despite Warriors-mania (and the viewing figures exclude All Blacks Tests), but you get the point: rugby league is a big thing across the ditch. These figures would be all too familiar to Australian rugby fans, and gallows humourists might conclude that Australia was always 10 years ahead of New Zealand.



What this all means for Australia is unclear. Powerbrokers from across the New Zealand rugby system will descend on Wellington next week to discuss their options, but identifying the issue is the easy part – finding agreement on a solution is far harder. However, there is a half-glass-full world in which the urgency of the Kiwis’ problems works in Australia’s favour. Rugby Australia CEO Phil Waugh with NZ Rugby counterpart Steve Lancaster at the Super Rugby Pacific launch earlier this year. Getty Images Certainly, there doesn’t seem to be any appetite from NZ Rugby to bin Super Rugby Pacific and return to a domestic competition, the NPC, as their elite competition model. The NZ Rugby document states that the preferred men’s elite competition “retains Trans-Tasman, with design able to expand”.



So, for example, if you are a private investor keen to put money into the NSW Waratahs, there is certainty that the Tahs will have a competition to play in. And, for example, if you are the Queensland Rugby Union and contemplating a split between the professional game and the community game with a view to investing into the Reds in a private Super Rugby model, that possibility still exists. But above and beyond the specifics, the common challenges facing Australia and New Zealand should promote a collegial attitude to addressing them. There is evidence that is already happening, with the Reds and Blues set to face each other on the Anzac Day weekend in Brisbane. A Bledisloe Cup Test will serve as the main event on April 25. The Herald has spoken to Reds chief executive David Hanham and his Blues counterpart Karl Budge in recent weeks, and both are on the same page about the opportunity that fixture presents, rather than looking at the Wallabies and All Blacks who won’t be available.



“I think we’ve got to reverse how we view these occasions,” Budge said. “I look at someone like young Cohen Norrie [Auckland and Blues five eighth/fullback]. In almost any other sport, he’d be considered a first-round draft pick. “When those first-round draft picks get a chance to finally debut for a club, it’s a sellout occasion in other sports. Super Rugby Pacific is forecast to lose about $NZ11 million in the 2025-2026 financial year. Getty Images “I’d rather reverse that conversation and go, ‘Isn’t it amazing that we’re going to finally get a chance to see Cohen Norrie rather than see Beauden Barrett’.” The other Super Rugby clubs will share similar attitudes regarding the preceding weekend, when they will also be missing their Test players.



The Wallabies and All Blacks will, of course, remain the primary teams for RA and NZR, the only outfits that actually make a bit of money. Related Article Australian rugby Waratahs’ firebrand could become a Springbok-style asset, says coach But both unions need to find a way to make a professional rugby competition below Test level at least sustainable from a commercial perspective. At present, it clearly is not. The NZ Rugby document revealed that Super Rugby Pacific is forecast to lose about $NZ11 million in the 2025-2026 financial year, while their Super Rugby Aupiki competition for women’s rugby will lose an eye-watering $NZ8.5 million.



NZ Rugby’s reduced broadcast deal with Sky is partly to blame, despite the robust viewing figures Super Rugby Pacific still attracts. Getting that competition right will be no mean feat, but RA and NZ Rugby are both now in the same position: they have to, or else. World.title: Freo storm into grand final after SCG thriller, but star of the show calls his goal ‘a fluke’
World.content:
Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce spoke to Kayo Sports post-game.

On making the grand final:

“It was hard to put into words. The game threw so much at us, and we were down for so long, but we just hung in their and hung in there. I didn’t have a sense of relief, it was just joy and pride. We were able to play our best footy when the pressure was at its highest, we were calm, went through our gears and individuals stepped up in the big moments.

Alex Pearce of the Dockers celebrates with fans. Getty Images

On whether it will sink in that he will captain the Dockers in the grand final next weekend:

“Probably not, well, actually it will. I’m human and I dream. I daydream about what it will be like. But I’m very conscious of that because wanting it doesn’t make it happen and dreaming about it doesn’t make it happen. Playing the footy we did in the last quarter will go along way to getting us the result we want.

On how the team will handle grand final week:

“As boring as it sounds, we will get through this, reset, review the game and look at what we did poorly and what we can improve on and how we were able to play our best footy in the end.

World.title: Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House Michael Koziol Updated September 19, 2026 — 6:38am ,first published 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump said he was banning cable news channel CNN and two other prominent US media outlets from the White House because of what he referred to as their “constant ‘reporting’ fake news”. The US president made the declaration on his social media platform Truth Social on Friday afternoon (Saturday morning AEST). He said MS-NOW, formerly known as MSNBC, was also banned, along with politics-focused news outlet Politico – which has just launched an Australian division. US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Friday afternoon. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote. He said the ban would be effective immediately. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”



The announcement is an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s long-standing animosity towards the media and outlets that report factual stories he does not like. It was not immediately clear exactly what Trump’s directive meant, as there are various levels of access that reporters have to the White House and the president. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in the White House press briefing room on the night a shooter targeted the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. AP Journalists are issued passes for the White House grounds, but that does not guarantee access to the “pool” - a smaller, rotating group of reporters that are allowed inside the Oval Office. CNN’s Kristen Holmes was still present and reporting from the White House on Friday afternoon.



Asked for clarification at a news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said: “I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. The ban would go as far as you can.” Trump suggested there was no particular trigger for his decision to ban the three outlets now. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said. “They purposefully write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.” Donald Trump takes questions from reporters in the Oval Office on Friday after announcing a ban on CNN, Politico and MS-NOW. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The president went on to cite his election victory and wins in all seven swing states, and suggested the banned outlets did not extend him enough praise. “I won [in] a landslide and I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart, I get it a little bit from Fox [News]. What I do ask is just a semblance of truth … everything’s been a victory. It has all been a victory.”



At one point, Trump was confused when a reporter attempted to ask him about the ban. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” he said. He later acknowledged: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” In his first term, Trump attempted to ban a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, by revoking his White House pass. CNN succeeded in having it restored via a legal challenge. CNN’s Kristen Holmes at the White House in April. She was still reporting from the White House grounds on Friday afternoon after the “ban”. Getty Images But in Trump’s second term, the White House has taken more control of the daily press pool, giving space to smaller, “new media” outlets that are typically conservative or even far-right. The White House Correspondents’ Association has traditionally managed the pool. WHCA president Jacqui Heinrich, who is from Fox News, said the group stood in defence of its colleagues at CNN, MS-NOW and Politico, who were being “singled out for doing their jobs”.



“The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” Heinrich said. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organisation’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask. “This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.” The White House press pool in the Oval Office on Friday. Bloomberg Founded in 1980, CNN provides close coverage of US politics, with several prominent reporters ordinarily based at the White House. Owned by Warner Bros Discovery, it is set to be sold to David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance as part of a $US110 billion ($154b) merger, though Paramount recently said selling the channel was an option to resolve market concentration issues in the deal. Trump has frequently targeted CNN for its coverage of his war against Iran and other matters. He has directed many attacks at high-profile anchor Kaitlan Collins, whom he called “very dumb and unhappy” last week. He regularly accuses her of failing to smile sufficiently.



Politico’s inclusion on the banned list was surprising given it is not a regular Trump target. In his Truth Social post, he dredged up an old complaint about the outlet receiving $US8 million from the Biden administration, suggesting it was “corruption”. In fact, the money was for subscriptions to Politico’s premium products. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer CNN said it stood behind its White House team and its fair and accurate reporting. “We have right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” the network said. “Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right.” There is currently no White House press secretary after Karoline Leavitt departed the role last month. She has not been replaced. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: How this team of experts guides 80-metre turbine blades down our roads with just millimetres to spare
World.content:
It is just after midnight on a winter morning when we gather at the Port of Newcastle.

In the background coal ships slink by, in the foreground an almost inconceivably vast wind turbine blade lies along the spine of a truck bed like some sort of alien life form strapped to a gurney in a sci-fi film.

It’s so big that it’s hard to fit it all into the frame of your eye from any reasonable perspective. At its tip it tapers to the length of schoolkid’s ruler. Towards that tapered end it has a jagged edge like a cartoon dragon’s teeth, a shape designed to reduce noise as it slices through the air. Peering up at its midsection, you could be looking at a warship’s prow from the ocean’s surface.

A team of transport specialists are making last-minute preparations to move this beast through the sleeping streets of suburban Newcastle and the coal villages of the Hunter Valley, along the Golden Highway to a hillside outside Wellington on the NSW Central Slopes, where it is to be raised upon a tower as part of a Squadron Energy wind farm that will soon be generating enough electricity for about 220,000 homes.

It seems absurd that this thing can be moved at all, let alone along busy roads, but the man in charge of this circus, Steve Spiller, seems impossibly calm. Jovial, even.

The police and pilots gather before the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Form and function

Wind turbine blades, explains engineer Dr Rosemary Barnes, are the largest single-component objects that humans regularly either build or seek to move. Artefacts of the modern world tend to shrink as technology advances, but wind turbines, shaped by both economic and physical forces, keep growing.

Longer turbine blades scoop up more wind and generate more electricity with each rotation, says Barnes, who has spent a career designing, building and repairing turbines and blades around the world and now runs a renewable energy consultancy. A dozen huge turbines need fewer gearboxes, less cable and wiring, less maintenance, less concrete and steel to generate as much electricity as dozens of small ones.

As the turbines grow in length, so do the forces exerted upon them. In extreme conditions, a large blade might bend 10 to 15 metres from a straight line. Imagine, says Barnes, a diving board wilting under the weight of a herd of elephants.

“They have to survive that transfer of force hundreds of millions of times over a life of about 30 years. Every time the blade is in the three o’clock position, gravity is bending it one way, and then when it goes into the nine o’clock position, it’s bending the exact opposite way, and it keeps repeating like that as it spins. It’s just like if you bend a paperclip back and forth repeatedly, you know that small load is not going to break it, but you do it enough times, and you get fatigue loading, it is going to break.”

All this means that not only must a blade be handmade from tough, light composite materials, they are stronger when they are crafted in a single piece, rather than disassembled for transport, which brings us back to Spiller and his crew in Newcastle.

The monster they are about to move is 82 metres long and weighs just over 20 tonnes.

The port

The crew is doing last-minute checks on vehicles and equipment. Craig Carpenter is inspecting the Kenworth truck and the purpose-built trailer he is about to drive. The trailer has a long spine that can be extended to suit its load, and six sets of axles at the rear.

The steerer, Freddie Scheepers, checks the truck prior to the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Tonight Carpenter’s load from front grille to blade tip will be 92 metres long. Carpenter picked up the nickname Blade Runner One for his smooth driving while moving blades in Western Australia last year, but just as crucial is Freddie Scheepers, who is “steerer” and will pursue Carpenter in a van close behind the truck.

Scheepers must not only keep his own vehicle on the road, but when necessary will use a remote control to steer the rear axles of the trailer. He keeps in constant contact with Carpenter so at any given moment the two know exactly where the blade tip is in relation to the road and the rest of the rig.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond. They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.” Steve Spiller, project manager

When the front of the rig moves upwards and is forcing the tip towards the ground, Scheepers will also be able to raise and lower the blade itself, the last metres of which rest in a hydraulic jack that sits over the axle sets.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond,” says Spiller, watching Carpenter and Scheepers make final preparations. “They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.”

Mayfield Macca’s

The convoy pulls out at about 1am. There are two police cars, as required by law when moving a load of this size in NSW. There are four pilot vehicles which help manage traffic around the truck and trailer. Scheepers’ steering van hunts along behind the blade like a sheepdog, and we follow in a four-wheel drive with Spiller, the project manager.

The turbine blade starts its journey from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Also in tow is a Transport NSW vehicle with a couple of observers, there to see if anything can be learnt or improved for future runs. After this, there are still another 195 blades to go, let alone the turbine hubs, tower sections and generators.

“When you pull back the curtain, this is what building a wind farm looks like – thousands of individual movements, decisions and people are needed to get every component to site,” Squadron Energy’s chief executive Rob Wheals later observes.

Steve Spiller, Ares Group project manager, accompanies the turbine blade on its journey from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

“At 80 metres long and shaped like a banana, each blade is one of the most challenging pieces of infrastructure to ever move.”

From Spiller’s radio we can hear occasional chatter from the pilot vehicles, but he leaves the “Bladerunners” to their own quiet comms channel so they can concentrate. Before we’ve even left the port precinct the blade tip sweeps out over a cyclone fence, clearing it by what seems like centimetres.

Spiller doesn’t flinch. Every move is rehearsed, every distance measured.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side on its journey from the Port of Newcastle to the wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

At a McDonald’s on a roundabout on Industrial Drive in the neighbouring suburb of Mayfield, the cop cars and pilot vehicles splay out to halt traffic coming from three directions, and Scheepers climbs out of his van to flick a switch on the rig to remote control. He adjusts the height of the suspension, and then he steers the rear of the rig around the turn.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side at the intersection of Industrial Drive and Maitland Road, Mayfield. Photo: Janie Barrett

Speed picks up, at least until the caravan reaches the Hunter Expressway. To make it onto that section, the pilots block traffic on the expressway in both directions while the Bladerunners navigate the rig 80 metres down an off-ramp into what would otherwise be oncoming traffic, then drive a kilometre down the wrong side of the road before crossing back. Spiller seems pleased by how smoothly this dance of traffic and truck is performed.

The remote used for steering the rear of the truck that carried the enormous turbine blade. Photo: Janie Barrett

As we head northwest towards the Golden Highway, Spiller relaxes enough to tell his story. He became an expert in moving big stuff almost by accident. At 19, he took a job with a logistics firm and began moving shipping containers. Half a decade later he was moving wind turbine parts, and the work took him around the world with the global giant GE. He has moved bits and pieces of wind farms by sea and land and even air, at one point chartering the world’s biggest aircraft, an Antonov, to move a wind turbine hub and six generators from Leipzig to Adelaide.

In Germany, near the Polish border, he recalls coaxing blades through tiny villages on a truck that could raise them to near vertical from the base to navigate tight spaces.

Freddie Scheepers changes the steering of the rear of the truck from manual to automatic via an external switch on the truck. Photo: Janie Barrett

In Australia, it’s easier because we have so much space. “I moved 300 blades through Toowoomba without complaint,” he boasts. Today he works for the Ares Group, which was contracted by GE, who built the blade at a factory in China, to shepherd it safely off the ship in Newcastle and on to the Squadron Energy site outside Wellington.

Despite the late hour you can tell the convoy is having an impact along the way. In one hamlet we pass within metres of the old coal miners’ cottages. A man in a dressing gown watches on in the pre-dawn from his veranda. His expression is impossible to read in the revolving lights.

Craig Carpenter, the truck driver who drove the turbine blade from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

From the sections of widened road you can see along the way the years of preparation that went into this operation. EnergyCo, the NSW government authority responsible for delivering the state’s five renewable energy zones, has spent $130 million preparing this route.



Inland

There are rules about moving oversized loads in the dark on the Golden Highway, so the convoy pulls over before dawn. A quiet pall descends across the still convoy, except for cheerful noises from Carpenter’s cabin. He hums and sings to himself and taps out a rhythm before drifting into silence.

In bright early light, against the country homes in Denman, the enormity of the blade begins to become clearer. It is longer than whole blocks of the little town. Along the Golden Highway, the convoy at times creeps up to something approaching normal traffic speed, and time passes quickly until we reach the site of the wind farm, headquartered on a sheep and cattle operation on rolling green hills east of Wellington.

As the truck prepares to tackle the narrow dirt roads built for the project we are taken into a sprawling site office for a safety induction. Whiteboards on the walls show the progress in the construction of each of the 69 turbines that will soon be operational here. There are posters boosting the “core values” of Squadron Energy, which is owned by Tattarang, the investment company that is in turn owned by Andrew Forrest and Nicola Forrest. The values include “Humility” and “Frugality”.

It is midafternoon on a hilltop I had last seen two years earlier when Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Forrest attended a sod-turning ceremony. Bladerunner One finally steps out of his cabin and offers up a great two-armed stretch to the sky. By now Spiller has left the site on his way back to his head office in Melbourne. Workers on-site scramble over the blade, breaking it free of its harnesses and lowering it into a cradle by a half-built tower. By the time it is operational it will stand 148 metres from base to blade tip.

There’s no getting around the impact the project is having on a beautiful landscape. Construction pads are scraped into the ground by each tower and the new roads hum with the sort of traffic flow you’d expect in a prosperous town.

The turbine blade arrives ar the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Later I ask farmer John Holland, owner of Uungula, for which the wind farm is named, what he makes of it all. He speaks with a careful, precise manner, aware of the controversy that wind projects attract. Squadron, he says, will clean up after the construction is complete, leaving him with new roads, giving even better access to the property’s ridge lines.

He says he has no fear about the impact of the turbines on his stock. Visiting other wind farms, he has seen sheep “camping” under the towers for shade. He reckons the turbines look majestic, but admits that when he saw renders of what they would look like spread across the land he loves he found it “a little confronting.”

He thinks renewable energy is a part of the solution for Australia’s growing energy demand, but not the only one. Like many farmers, he opposes grid-scale solar plants taking up agricultural land. But he has practical considerations too. The rent Squadron will pay for each turbine will let the family retire a fair chunk of debt, though he won’t say how much. Nor will he say how many turbines his farm will host. “That’s a bit like asking how much money I’ve got in the bank. It’s a bit rude.”

But he is happy to say the income has helped settle the questions of succession that can cause such grief to farming families, and to update equipment and improve fences and dams.

“It’s the confidence to be able to run the property the way it should be run.”

I ask him what Uungula means.

“It’s an Aboriginal word,” he says. “It means wind in the hills.”

Workers unload the turbine blade after its long journey. Photo: Janie Barrett

Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Man left unconscious and another in custody after assault in Gisborne
World.content:
An early morning assault in Gisborne left a man unconscious and requiring hospital treatment on Saturday.

Police said the injured man has since been discharged and an 18-year-old man is in custody.

Police are appealing for information on the incident after they were called to the city's Peel Street about 2am on Saturday following reports a man had been knocked unconscious.

The 18-year-old in custody was assisting with enquiries, a police spokesperson said.

"As part of those enquiries, we'd like to hear from anybody who witnessed the incident," the spokesperson said.

"We understand a number of people were present at the time of the assault who may also have video footage."

Anyone with information or video footage is urged to contact the police on 105, either over the phone or online at 105.police.govt.nz, referencing file number 260919/1079.
